source.title: Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Personalization
source.authors: Sekh Mainul Islam; Pepa Atanasova; Isabelle Augenstein

record.tranche_reason: Uses k-sparse probing, rather than the original neuron-level visual analysis, to compare how sparsely personalization concepts are decodable in MoE and dense language models; the authors interpret the results as evidence about polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The polysemanticity-relevant result is the k-sparse probe comparison in Figure 3. Other reported personalization, crosscoder, explanation, routing, and causal-intervention results concern personalization performance or feature localization, not whether neurons are polysemantic. Figure 3 reports probe results across k=64 to k=1; the text specifically describes the result at k=1 but gives no exact plotted values.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It takes reduced polysemanticity in MoE LLMs as a premise (citing Yang 2025b and Herbst 2026) to motivate its crosscoder method. Its one 'polysemanticity' result is k-sparse probe balanced accuracy on 20 personalization concepts (Fig. 3). That shows how few units decode a concept, not whether units respond to unrelated inputs or what share of neurons is polysemantic. It is a related but different construct. The comparison is also confounded: MoE gets best-of-many expert selection, and the dense comparators have different pretraining recipes.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that MoE LLMs show lower polysemanticity than dense LLMs with similar active parameters for personalization. They base this on k-sparse probes (gap wide at k=1) and on crosscoder ν ratios, which hold within the same family except Mixtral. They caution that probes measure decodability, not use, and that best-of-many selection favours MoE, particularly at k=1. They also note that dense comparators differ in pretraining data and recipes.
record.recipe_differences: Uses k-sparse probing of personalization concepts in language-model neurons, not the original visual neuron-feature demonstrations.
record.method_sensitivity: Probe results are reported over k values from 64 to 1. The authors note that the MoE–dense gap remains wide at k=1.

fits_no_version.finding: In k-sparse probes for 20 personalization concepts, MoE experts' top-k neurons give higher balanced accuracy than matched-active-parameter dense MLPs, with the gap wide even at k=1. Values are figure-only, and selection effects favour MoE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concepts are decodable from fewer units in MoE expert neurons than in dense MLP neurons of similar active size.

fits_no_version.finding: Personalized crosscoder latents explain the non-personalized model less (lower ν) in MoE than in same-family dense models. Mixtral is the exception: higher ν than Llama-2-13B (Fig. 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning-specific crosscoder latents are less shared with the base model in MoE than in dense LLMs.

record.problems: Figure 3 provides the probe values only graphically, without exact values in the text. The study probes 20 personalization concepts and does not directly count polysemantic neurons. The authors note that response-level concepts are assigned token-level labels, introducing noise; selecting the best component may favor MoE models because they have more candidates, and selection effects may remain, particularly at k=1. Probes measure decodability, not use.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows left out. Personalization performance tables and other analyses were excluded because they do not measure polysemanticity or the k-sparse probe outcome.

untested.parts: No share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens, and no layer-wise variation.
No measured share of polysemantic neurons under architecture changes. The MoE vs dense probe comparison is a different construct and is confounded by pretraining differences.
Not examined. The auto-interp F1 rising across activation bins concerns crosscoder latents, not neurons.

record.verdict_notes: All probe values are figure-only. The paper's polysemanticity framing relies on cited prior work rather than a direct measurement of neuron polysemanticity, so the reader's V5 'supports' label is removed.

versions.untested_parts: Image-classifier neurons and mixed visual inputs.
The share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and variation in that share across language-model layers.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons, or by superposition.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when there is enough capacity.

SoLU, modern convolutional networks, regularization changes, and direct measurement of the share of polysemantic neurons or associated performance costs. The study compares MoE and dense models on a personalization probe.
Whether canonical mixed-meaning neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs rather than unrelated inputs.
Whether polysemanticity classifications change with activation-range selection or explanation scoring; the k-sparse probe sweep is not a direct count of such classifications.

relation.reason: The study uses reduced polysemanticity in MoE as motivation. Its probe measures concept localization/decodability, not the share of polysemantic neurons, so it does not test V5.

tranche.reason: The study takes MoE's lower polysemanticity (Yang 2025b, Herbst 2026) as the premise for its crosscoder/expert analysis. Its own 'polysemanticity' result (Fig. 3) is best-of-many k-sparse probe decodability of persona concepts. The paper itself says sparse probing 'measures how few neurons encode a concept'. That is not the share of neurons responding to unrelated inputs. MoE probes use only tokens routed to a selected expert, and the authors say selection favours MoE, especially at k=1. Under verdict_rules §1 a related but different construct is not a test.

source_check.notes: The k-sparse values in Fig. 3 are plot-only. The text says only that MoE beats active-matched dense LLMs on balanced accuracy, with a wider gap within family (OLMo, Qwen) and a gap that stays wide at k=1. Authors' caveats: selection favours MoE, probes show decodability not use, and dense comparators differ in pretraining. The 'Chance' baseline on the rows comes from the Fig. 7 legend.

statements.problem: none. The study is correctly not counted as a verdict-bearing test. Its probed models fit the size bins: OLMoE-1B-7B (6.9B total), Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-30B-A3B (30B), Mixtral-8x7B (46.7B), Llama-2-13B. None is above 100B.

Minor: the basis's by_family count lists OLMo, Qwen and Mistral but not Llama-2-13B, which Fig. 3 also probes. The basis's own parenthetical does name Llama13, and the statement's claim holds because the study is not a test.
